title: TB9-06392
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant), a citizen of Nigeria, and XXXX XXXX XXXX (Associate Appellant), a citizen of the United States of America (USA) and Nigeria, appealed a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated February 7, 2019. The RPD rejected their claims for refugee protection due to negative credibility findings.

The Appellants allege that they fear returning to Nigeria as the husband of the Appellant, who is also the father of the Associate Appellant, was discovered to have had a homosexual relationship in the past. The Appellants allege that they face retribution as a result of this relationship. The Appellants further allege that the RPD erred when assessing the credibility of their claims. The Appellants have not submitted new evidence and have not requested an oral hearing.

I find that the Appellant is not credible. I further find that the Appellants have not established their claims. The Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor are they persons in need of protection. The Appeal is dismissed.

While reviewing the RPD decision, I am required to independently determine whether the RPD was correct in relation to each alleged error of law, fact or mixed fact and law. I may defer to the RPD's credibility assessment of the oral testimony if I find that the RPD had a meaningful advantage in the circumstances.1 Reasons will be provided in my analysis if I find that the RPD had a meaningful advantage.
When assessing this claim, I was guided by the Chairperson's Guideline 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution (Gender Guideline).2

I find that the Appellant was not a credible witness and that she has not established her claims. My reasons for these findings are below. The Appellant has not established that her husband is bisexual. The Appellant gave no testimony or evidence regarding her husband's sexuality

The Appellant argues that the RPD based its findings on speculation that the Appellant's husband is not bisexual because his refugee claim was rejected by both the RPD and the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD). The Appellant argues that the RPD failed to evaluate her fears subjectively as detailed in her Basis of Claim (BOC) and the supporting documentation.

The RPD found that, although the RPD and RAD decision regarding the claim of her husband did not form part of the record,3 the Appellant acknowledged having read both decisions, and testified that his claim was not accepted because he was not believed. The RPD also considered the application of the Minister's counsel which attempted to have these decisions included in the record, and found that the Appellant's husband was not granted refugee protection because he lacked credibility. The RPD found that, given that the Appellant is relying on an allegation by her husband that he has been targeted for an earlier homosexual relationship which has been found to be not credible, the presumption that sworn testimony is true has already been rebutted.4

The RPD noted that the Appellant could have called her husband as a witness, and could have filed or allowed evidence from his claim to be considered in her proceeding, but chose not to do so. The RPD further noted that the Appellant filed no corroborative evidence to establish that her husband was sought by police, or that his business was attacked and looted in XXXX 2017. The RPD drew a significant negative inference from the absence of this evidence.

When asked about the homosexual relationship that allegedly exposed the Appellant's husband's sexual orientation in Nigeria, the Appellant stated that she did not remember or know if she ever really talked to her husband about that man, but that she knew he was a childhood friend who went to school with her husband as a child.5 Throughout the hearing, when asked about evidence of her husband's sexuality, the Appellant stated that her husband told her that he is bisexual, and he has no reason to lie to her.

I am aware of the Chairperson's Guideline 9: Proceedings Before the IRB Involving Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity and Expression6 (SOGIE Guideline) which states that: 3.2 An individual's testimony may be the only evidence of their SOGIE where, in a given case, corroborative or additional evidence is not reasonably available.

However, given that the Appellant's husband was in Canada with her at the time of the hearing, and given that the Appellant did not allow her husband's decisions or the evidence from those decisions to be part of the record, I find that the RPD did not err by taking a negative inference from the complete lack of evidence to corroborate her allegation that her husband is bisexual. While it is true that the only evidence of an individual's SOGIE may be their testimony, I find that the RPD was not even afforded the testimony of the individual who is claiming to be bisexual. I take a negative inference from the absence of testimony and evidence regarding the Appellants' core allegation.

While I do not find that the RPD was correct to find that the RPD and the RAD must have found that the Appellant's husband's claims were not credible, I do find that the RPD was correct to find that the presumption of truth has been rebutted, as the Appellant has adduced no evidence of her husband's sexuality, and she was unable to testify about his same-sex relationship on his behalf. The Appellant gave contradictory testimony regarding her knowledge of her husband's refugee claim

The RPD found that the Appellant admitted that her husband told her about making a claim in Canada while she was pregnant and living in the USA. The RPD found that her testimony regarding her husband's refugee claim was vague and contradictory.

The Appellant argues that she cannot be held to every statement and required to remember all facts as a person who is fleeing persecution, as this will amount to requiring her to prove her case beyond a reasonable doubt.

In her BOC narrative, the Appellant stated that: While in the USA I asked my husband when he was returning to Nigeria and he kept on postponing the date claiming that he had business to take care of in Canada. After my delivery my daughter and I came back to Canada on XXXX XXXX 2017 to join him with the mind that we would go back to Nigeria together... He told me on XXXX XXXX, 2017 that had a confession to make and I encouraged him to talk. He said he didn't want to tell me when I visited in XXXX XXXX - XXXX XXXX, 2017 because of my medical condition. He disclosed to me that he's bisexual and informed me that he had a homosexual relationship... After about a week I sat him down and spoke my mind to him...he informed me that he had made a claim for refugee protected in Canada, gone for a hearing and the claim but was not accepted and that he has filed an Appeal...

In contrast, during testimony, the Appellant stated that her husband told her in XXXX of 2017 that he had made a refugee claim but that she was not interested and just wanted to focus on being healthy as she was pregnant.7 The RPD asked for her to confirm that her husband told her about the claim while she was still pregnant, and she confirmed that yes, he just said something about making a claim, and she was just focused on being healthy.8 The Minister's counsel later confirmed this order of events when questioning the Appellant as to why she did not make a claim in the USA when she found out that her husband was making a claim in Canada. The Appellant stated that she did not make a claim in the USA as she was focused on having her baby, and she did not yet know about her husband's sexuality.9

The Appellant's testimony contradicted the order of events of how she found out about two important things: her husband's refugee claim, and his sexuality as outlined in her BOC. Given that her claim is based on her husband's sexuality, I find that this contradiction is regarding her core allegation. Even if I accept that she found out her husband had taken the significant step of making a refugee claim and in response she asked for no further details, I find that she would be able to recall the order of how she found out about those two extremely significant pieces of information. I take a negative credibility inference from this contradictory testimony. On a balance of probabilities, I find that the Appellant's husband did not sit her down on XXXX XXXX, 2017 to tell her he was bisexual. I find that this further undermines the Appellant's claim that her husband is bisexual. The Appellant has not established her newer claims of retribution she has allegedly experienced as a result of her husband's sexuality The Appellant has not established that her father has disinherited her

The RPD found that the Appellant has not established that her father is a Muslim extremist, or that it would benefit him in his political aspirations in becoming the XXXX of Nigeria to make an example of the Appellant and the Associate Appellant. The RPD found that the timing of the affidavit from the Appellant's father on XXXX XXXX, 2018, is highly suspect as well as being internally inconsistent.

The RPD further found that whether or not the affidavit was sworn by the Appellant's father, the RPD did not find it credible that the affidavit was made for the benefit of his supporters. The RPD found that the affidavit was created in order to bolster the Appellant's refugee claim following the dismissal of her husband's appeal.

The RPD found that, given that the Appellant claims that she was being disinherited by her father because of his extremist Muslim views and intolerance for homosexuality, and to show his Muslim supporters how strict he is, the Appellant could not credibly explain why her father would disinherit her because of her disregard for her Christian faith as stated at the top of the affidavit.

The Appellant argues that the RPD impugned her credibility on the issue of her father not being an extremist, and that the affidavit was not controverted yet the member chose to ignore such important evidence and went into speculation.

During testimony, the Appellant was asked to explain why her father's affidavit states that he is disinheriting her partly due to her disregard for Christian faith, when the Appellant is alleging that her father is a rigid Muslim extremist. Her first response was that this was a biblical reference to Sodom and Gomorrah, as this is where Nigeria's anti-homosexual laws originally derived the name of the offence of sodomy.10 Later in the hearing, when asked the same question by her counsel, the Appellant stated that she was married as a Christian, because if she had married as a Muslim she would have had to wear a niqab, so her father refused to walk her down the aisle.11

I do not find that either of these responses are consistent with each other, nor do they explain why her father would reference her disregard for Christian faith in an affidavit meant to convince his followers that he is a devout Muslim. I take a negative credibility inference from this part of the father's affidavit and from the Appellant's inability to consistently or credibly explain this part of the father's affidavit.

In testimony, the Appellant stated that her father called her on her birthday in XXXX of 2018. The Appellant further testified that it was during this phone call that her father stated that she should know that from now on that she is not his daughter and she will never have his protection anywhere in Nigeria.

When asked when her husband's appeal was decided, the Appellant stated that she did not remember. When suggested to her that it was sometime in the fall of 2018, the Appellant again stated that she did not remember.12

On a balance of probabilities, I find that the timing of the father's affidavit indicates that this document was created to bolster the Appellant's claim. Given this finding, and the credibility finding regarding the content of this document above, I give this document no weight in establishing the Appellant's claims that her father has disinherited her. The Appellant has not established that her shop was attacked

The RPD found that it was highly suspect that the Appellant received an email on XXXX XXXX, 2018, concerning an attack on her shop on XXXX XXXX, 2018. The RPD drew an adverse inference from the failure of the Appellant to file any other objective evidence to support that her business was attacked as alleged, and found that she gave contradictory evidence about whether or not she was involved with the business, and whether the person who allegedly emailed her about the attack was an employee, or otherwise directly connected with a business that was associated with the Appellant.

The Appellant did not contest these findings. I have listened to the corresponding testimony13 and have reviewed the email14. I have found no errors in the RPDs findings. I therefore adopt these findings as my own. I further find that the Appellant has not established that her business was attacked, nor has she established that her business was attacked due to her husband's sexuality. The RPD did not contradict the Gender Guideline.

The Appellants allege that the RPD did not apply the Gender Guideline in the hearing or in the decision-making process. The Appellants did not provide any examples of where the application of this guideline would have altered the RPD's findings. I have reviewed the RPD's decision and I found no examples of where the Gender Guideline was not applied, or where directly applying the Gender Guideline would have altered the RPD's decision. The Appellant is not a Convention refugee, nor is she a person in need of protection

I find that the Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that her husband is bisexual or that she has faced any consequences of his alleged sexuality. I conclude that the Appellant would not face a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground should she return to Nigeria.

For the same reasons, I conclude that, on a balance of probabilities, the Appellant would not be subjected to a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual punishment, or a danger of torture, should she return to Nigeria. The Associate Appellant is not a convention refugee or a person in need of protection

XXXX XXXX XXXX is an American citizen. No independent claim was raised against the US on her behalf. No new allegation has been raised as part of the appeal. For these reasons, I find that she is not a convention refugee nor is she a person in need of protection.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
